title: Lecture #18: AutoBoxing, Abstract classes & POJOs
topics: POJO: anemic vs rich domain model

questions.question: For `int x = 10; Integer y = x;` and later `int z = y;`, what does the compiler actually do, per the lecture?
options: Both lines copy the raw int; Integer is just another name for int
`Integer y = x` becomes `Integer.valueOf(x)` (autoboxing) and `int z = y` becomes `y.intValue()` (unboxing)
`Integer y = x` becomes `y.intValue()` (unboxing) and `int z = y` becomes `Integer.valueOf(y)` (autoboxing)
Both lines are compile errors without an explicit cast like `(Integer) x`
questions.explanation: Integer is a wrapper class whose object holds an int `value`. Converting a primitive to its wrapper is autoboxing (compiled as `Integer.valueOf(x)`, the newer replacement for `new Integer(x)`), and extracting the primitive is unboxing (`intValue()`). The compiler inserts both automatically, so no casts are needed.

questions.question: Demo2 lists three places where boxing/unboxing happens: assignments, method calls and arithmetic. What does this print?
options: Compile error: `+` cannot be applied to two Integer objects
Compile error: an int cannot be passed to a parameter of type Integer
questions.explanation: `a + b` unboxes both Integers (arithmetic), giving 30; passing `sum` to `printInteger(Integer)` autoboxes it (method call); `x + 1` unboxes again and adds numerically, printing 31. No String is involved, so there is no concatenation like '301'.

questions.question: The lecture's Demo.java contains `public class Demo` plus `class Sample {}` and `class Sample2 {}`. Which statement is correct?
options: It compiles into Demo.class, Sample.class and Sample2.class; only Demo may be public, because a public class must be in a file with its own name, so the JVM can find `Demo.main()` from Demo.java
It fails to compile, because a .java file may contain only one class
It compiles into a single Demo.class that contains all three classes
It would also compile if Sample were made public, as long as Demo stays public
questions.explanation: A file may hold several top-level classes, and each gets its own .class file, but at most one may be public and it must match the file name (Demo.java -> Demo). That rule is what lets the tools map file to class, as the comment `Demo.java -> Demo.main()` hints. Making Sample public too would require a file named Sample.java.

questions.question: What happens when this part of Demo2 runs?
options: Prints 0, because null unboxes to the int default value
Prints null
Compile error: null cannot be assigned to an Integer
Throws NullPointerException at `int y = x;`
questions.explanation: A wrapper reference may be null, so `Integer x = null` compiles. Unboxing compiles to `x.intValue()`, and calling a method on null throws NullPointerException at run time. Java never silently converts null to 0, and an int can never hold null.

questions.question: In Demo4, `abstract class Animal` has a constructor `Animal(String name)`, yet `new Animal(...)` is not allowed. Which statement is correct?
options: The constructor is useless and is silently ignored by the compiler
The constructor runs when a subclass constructor calls it, e.g. `Dog(String name) { super(name); }`, to initialize the inherited `name` field
Abstract classes cannot declare constructors, so Demo4 does not compile
The constructor makes Animal instantiable as long as it has a parameter
questions.explanation: Demo4's Q&A says abstract classes can have constructors. They are never used directly with `new`, but every subclass object is partly an Animal, so `super(name)` in Dog runs Animal's constructor to set the shared state. Having parameters does not make the class instantiable; `abstract` alone forbids `new Animal(...)`.

questions.topic: POJO: anemic vs rich domain model
questions.question: Your `Student` POJO has only fields, a constructor and getters/setters. A teammate adds a `markAttendance()` method that applies attendance rules inside the class. In the lecture's terms, what changed?
options: It moved from an anemic model (data + getters/setters only) to a rich domain model (also contains business logic)
It moved from a rich domain model to an anemic model, because it now has more methods
It stopped being a class and became an interface
Nothing; any class with methods is called an anemic model
questions.explanation: The notes split POJOs into the anemic model (getters/setters, constructors, fields only) and the rich domain model, which also carries business logic such as `markAttendance()`. Adding behaviour with rules is what makes it 'rich'; it is still an ordinary plain Java class.

questions.question: A teammate compares two `Integer` order IDs with `if (id1 == id2)`. All tests with IDs 1 to 100 pass, but in production two orders with ID 5000 are reported as different. What is the cause and fix?
options: Integer overflows above 127; switch the IDs to `long`
`==` on Integer compares values only up to 1000; use `>=` and `<=` instead
`==` compares references; autoboxed values from -128 to 127 come from a shared cache (same object), larger ones are separate objects; compare with `id1.equals(id2)`
The JVM randomly reuses objects; the comparison must be wrapped in a try/catch
questions.explanation: As the lecture shows, `Integer.valueOf` returns cached objects for -128..127, so `==` happens to be true for small values, while 200 (or 5000) creates distinct objects and `==` gives false. `equals()` compares the wrapped int values (`this.value == y.value`). Integer does not overflow at 127; that is the byte range.

questions.question: With default JVM settings, what does this print?
options: true true true true
true false false true
false false true true
true false true true
questions.explanation: 127 is inside the -128..127 cache, so a and b are the same object (true); 128 is outside, so c and d are different objects (false). In `c == e` one side is a primitive int, so c is unboxed and the values are compared numerically (true). `equals` compares values (true). Treating `c == e` as a reference comparison gives the tempting wrong 'false'.

questions.question: Old code in your project creates wrappers with `new Integer(x)`, while the lecture marks `Integer.valueOf(x)` as the new way. A teammate asks what actually differs. What is the best answer?
options: `valueOf` may return a shared cached object (always for -128..127), saving memory and allocation, while `new Integer(x)` always creates a fresh object, so `new Integer(5) == new Integer(5)` is false (the constructor is deprecated)
There is no difference: both always return a brand-new object, so `==` behaves the same
`new Integer(x)` uses the cache, while `valueOf` always creates a new object, so `valueOf` is slower
`valueOf` returns a primitive int, while `new Integer(x)` returns an object
questions.explanation: Autoboxing compiles to `Integer.valueOf`, which hands out cached Integer objects for -128..127 (the stack/heap diagram in the notes shows several variables pointing to the same cached 100). The `new` operator always allocates a new object, so two of them are never `==`; the constructor has been deprecated since Java 9 for this reason. `valueOf` returns an Integer object, not a primitive.

questions.question: A variation of Demo4 calls an overridable method from the abstract class's constructor. What does `new Dog("Bruno");` print?
options: Animal sound Dog
Animal Bruno-bark Dog
Dog Animal Bruno-bark
Animal null-bark Dog
questions.explanation: `super(name)` runs Animal's constructor first: it sets `name` to "Bruno", prints 'Animal', then calls `makeSound()`. The object being built is a Dog, so the overridden Dog version runs even from inside the parent constructor, printing 'Bruno-bark' (name was already assigned). Then Dog's constructor body prints 'Dog'. 'sound' would require calls inside constructors to ignore overriding, which they do not.
